wa_stevens_pass_region.blurb: The Skykomish Valley runs along Highway 2 on the west side of the Cascades, where the river's two forks join near the small village of Index. The rock is granite, and the area is best known for two things: tall walls above Index and a huge amount of bouldering. Boulder problems outnumber roped routes, with a broad spread from easy warm-ups to hard testpieces. On rope, trad is more common than sport, and most lines sit between 5.10 and 5.12, with a fair number of easier ones too. Index offers single-pitch lines and longer multi-pitch climbs on south-facing walls that dry quickly after winter weather but can bake in summer. Gold Bar and the Miller River boulders hold fine-grained boulders in the forest, and Treasury is another sizeable sub-area. A railway passes close to the main wall, so expect train noise.

ar_north_central_arkansas.blurb: North-central Arkansas covers the Ozark and Boston Mountains country around Jasper, Mount Judea and the Buffalo National River, where the climbing is on sandstone. Sport routes make up about half of the climbing, with trad and a big helping of bouldering making up most of the rest. Grades are centred on the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with a decent number of moderates and a modest tail of harder lines, while boulder problems run from very easy through V8 and beyond. Horseshoe Canyon Ranch is the busiest sub-area, with mostly bolted lines, some trad and plenty of boulders. Sam's Throne is a hard-sandstone area in the national forest with a strong trad reputation, and its tops are reached with some scrambling. Cowell, Big Piney and Richland Creek add more outcrops spread through the hills and hollows.

ma_eastern_ma.blurb: Eastern Massachusetts is a scatter of small, mostly wooded crags and boulder fields in and around greater Boston, many of them easy to reach by transit or a short drive. Bouldering dominates, with plenty of problems at the easy end of the scale, and a good number of top-rope lines on top of that. Roped climbing is short and mostly moderate, with some harder trad and only a few sport lines. Hammond Pond is a rare conglomerate crag known for crack climbing. Quincy Quarries is a long-standing training ground with walls up to roughly 80 feet and mostly top-rope and trad lines. Middlesex Fells has drawn boulderers in recent years, and further out Gilbert Hills, Townsend, Milford and Rattlesnake Rocks add more boulders. It suits quick after-work sessions rather than big-wall days.

on_ontario_south_bouldering_and_rock.blurb: Southern Ontario's climbing is strung along the Niagara Escarpment, a long limestone ridge that runs from the Niagara area up to the Bruce Peninsula, with further crags such as Calabogie and Bon Echo to the east. Sport routes lead, followed by trad and a solid amount of bouldering, with a small winter scene of ice and mixed climbing. Most roped climbing falls between 5.9 and 5.12, with easy and moderate lines at the beginner-friendly crags near Milton. The Golden Horseshoe is the biggest cluster, and the Beaver Valley holds Devil's Glen, Metcalfe Rock and The Swamp. Lion's Head, up on the peninsula, offers harder climbing with Georgian Bay views and is better suited to experienced parties. Approaches are often steep or trailless, and phone coverage is patchy, so carry a printed topo and plan carefully.

co_boulder_canyon.blurb: Boulder Canyon cuts west from the edge of Boulder along the creek, with steep granite walls on both sides. It is one of the most developed canyons on the Front Range, with trad slightly ahead of sport and a smaller amount of bouldering and winter ice. Grades are centred on the 5.9 to 5.12 range, with plenty of moderates and a thinner tail of hard lines. Climbs go from short single-pitch crags to multi-pitch routes, and the walks in are usually short, though many crags sit across the creek and call for a creek crossing and a steep scramble. Castle Rock and the Elephant Buttresses are classic spots for trad, while the Sport Park and Lower Dream Canyon draw bolt-clippers. North-side walls catch winter sun but get very hot in summer, while the south-side walls stay cold and shady in winter and suit the heat.

bc_okanagan.blurb: The Okanagan is the dry, lake-filled valley country of interior British Columbia, running from Penticton north through Kelowna toward Vernon. Sport climbing is by far the main attraction, with trad second and a small bouldering scene. Most routes sit in the 5.9 to 5.12 range, with a decent number of easier ones and a trailing handful at the top end. Skaha Bluffs, above Skaha Lake near Penticton, is the standout, with coarse-grained gneiss walls generally under 30 metres tall, spread across a few parallel canyons. Further north, Cougar Canyon and Aberdeen Columns add more crags, and around Kelowna you will find Mount Boucherie, Lonely Crags and a very large boulderfield. The valley has mild weather by Canadian standards.
